title: 120/240 V overhead service, 25 kVA pole transformer, drop and meter base

sources.citation: real-world (the shipped utility stand-in's source, vetted in P2 and again in the P4 pre-audit, ADR 0021; not re-read for this entry): a single-phase pole-mounted distribution transformer serving one to a few homes is commonly 25 kVA, with an impedance of about 1.5–3 % and an X/R of about 1–3 (published manufacturers' data and utility service guides, paraphrased). 2 % and X/R 2 are taken: the full winding's impedance is 0.02 × 240² / 25 000 = 46.08 mΩ. Its line-to-neutral source is the half-winding T-equivalent (Kersting's centre-tapped approximation, ADR 0021 §1): about 8.23 kA line-to-neutral and 5.21 kA line-to-line at the transformer terminals with an infinite primary (an upper bound).
120 V from each line to the neutral (the secondary's centre tap), the 120/240 V single-phase three-wire nominal system of ANSI C84.1-2020 (cited by number; the region profile's split-phase system).

real-world and game-design: an overhead triplex service drop of two insulated 2 AWG aluminium line conductors and a bare neutral messenger, here one size smaller (4 AWG). Triplex drops are made with compressed 1350-H19 aluminium line conductors and a messenger of 6201 alloy, ACSR or aluminium, either full-size or reduced (makers' product listings, seen through search summaries, not read in full); the reduced neutral is a game-design choice among them. The areas are the AWG definition's (NBS Handbook 100's geometry, read in the P3 pre-audit): d = 0.127 mm × 92^((36 − n)/39), so 2 AWG is 6.5437 mm and 33.631 mm², 4 AWG 5.1894 mm and 21.151 mm². The messenger is taken at the line conductors' 1350 resistivity: a labelled abstraction (a 6201 messenger, about 52.5 % IACS, is about 16 % more resistive than 1350; a 4 AWG neutral at 1350 sits between a 2 AWG and a 4 AWG 6201 messenger).

NBS Handbook 109, Aluminum Wire Tables (1972; read in full by electrical-realism-reviewer, the pinned materials row aluminiumAa8000): aluminium at 61.0 % IACS has a resistivity of 2.8264 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m and a temperature coefficient of 0.00403 per kelvin at 20 °C (293.15 K). 1350-H19 conductor aluminium is specified at a minimum 61.0 % IACS (ASTM B230, cited by number, paywalled, not read). The drop's resistance is derived, ρL/A × (1 + α ΔT), never tabulated: 25.212 mΩ per line and 40.089 mΩ for the neutral over 30 m at 20 °C.

game-design: a 30 m span from the pole to the house's meter base (a typical overhead drop span; utilities set the limits in their service guides, not read). The drop's reactance is left out (ADR 0021, a labelled abstraction): about 0.1 Ω/km of triplex reactance, left out, would lower the meter-base fault currents by a few per cent (about 1.6 % L–N, 3.7 % L–L). The drop has no thermal node in P4.

game-design inside a sourced range (the P4 pre-audit, ADR 0021's reference notes): the transformer neutral's grounding to remote earth at the pole, 5 Ω, inside the 1–25 Ω of a multigrounded utility neutral and a single made electrode's 25 Ω ceiling (IEEE C2, the National Electrical Safety Code, Rule 096, cited by number).

game-design: drawn as the meter base the drop lands in, 280 × 370 × 120 mm, about the 11 × 14.5 in face of a 200 A-class single-phase ringless overhead meter socket (a meter-socket maker's catalogue, read 2026-11-18; its depth's fraction illegible in the text, about 4½–5 in). The load-side lugs l1, n and l2 sit side by side low in the can and take the service-entrance conductors downwards (−y). x0, the transformer neutral at the pole, is shown at the top and is unreachable (access none, a service.splitPhase rule): nothing lands or clips on it.

real-world (read 2026-11-18) and game-design: a meter-socket maker's catalogue lists the line and load connectors of its single-phase ringless sockets as copper-or-aluminium (CU/AL) lugs for #6–2/0 AWG on the 125 A class and #6 AWG–350 kcmil on the 200 A class, tin-plated extruded aluminium, one conductor each. The game narrows them to 2 AWG–4/0 (P4 plan F4.2 part 2), inside the 200 A class, so both the 2 AWG and the 4/0 aluminium service-entrance conductors land; stranded only (service-entrance sizes are stranded); one conductor per lug.

game-design: the fictional meter base's marked lug torque, 31 N·m (about 275 lb·in), of the order makers mark on socket-head lugs of this size class (seen only in search summaries; not read); the meter-socket catalogue read says the interior label's torque governs, and NFPA 70-2023 Art. 110.14(D) requires the marked value (both cited by number). No UL 486A-B torque table is used. The 5–70 N·m click torque wrench (tool.calderyn-tw-70) reaches it.

game-design: a 25 ± 3 mm strip and a 22 mm barrel grip for a 2 AWG–4/0 box lug, and a hexagon-socket set screw (hexSocket): meter-socket lugs of this size commonly take a hex key (common practice); the drive size isn't modelled.

game-design: a 2 AWG–4/0 lug's contact resistance at the marked torque, copper at 20 °C, 0.05 mΩ, a sixth of the 14–10 AWG screw class's 0.3 mΩ (NBS BSS 103) for its much larger clamped area (at 100 A it drops 5 mV, 0.5 W); a 0.2 W/K heat path (the screw class's scaled for a large lug and its conductor, not calibrated) and a 22 J/K lug, a physics estimate: about 25 g of tin-plated aluminium × 897 J/(kg·K).
